screens.title: Advanced VPC Connectivity: Peering, Transit Gateway, PrivateLink
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we’re going to build a mental model for three ways AWS lets VPCs talk to each other: VPC Peering, Transit Gateway, and PrivateLink. I’ll help you see where each service fits, what operational work they demand, and where people commonly make mistakes. You’ll learn a concrete example that shows why a small mesh of peering connections becomes painful at scale, how Transit Gateway centralizes routing for hub‑and‑spoke architectures, and when PrivateLink is the right way to expose a service securely across accounts without opening public endpoints. This matters because the connectivity method you choose affects cost, manageability, and security controls. For instance, a simple peering link is cheap and direct for two VPCs but quickly multiplies routing work as the environment grows. Transit Gateway reduces that operational cost at the price of centralized configuration and higher service cost. PrivateLink moves traffic over AWS private networks to present a service via an interface endpoint, avoiding CIDR coordination and public exposure. As you move through the screens you’ll see the essential configuration steps, common troubleshooting checks, and a hands‑on scenario that ties these ideas together. By the end you should be able to pick the right connectivity option for a real multi‑account architecture and explain why.

keyIdea.text: Peering for point‑to‑point simplicity, Transit Gateway for scalable hub‑and‑spoke routing, and PrivateLink for secure service exposure without public internet.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Advanced VPC Connectivity
Advanced VPC Connectivity
Peering, Transit Gateway, and PrivateLink — pick the right tool for scale, security, and manageability.
In this lesson
  • Understand non‑transitive peering and when it fails at scale.
  • Learn Transit Gateway attachments, route tables, and propagation.
  • See PrivateLink mechanisms for secure service exposure via ENIs and NLBs.
Coming up
Peering
Simple point‑to‑point connect, non‑transitive.
Transit Gateway
Hub for many VPCs with centralized routing.
PrivateLink
Expose services privately via interface endpoints.
Visual concept
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Peering mesh
Many direct links grow quadratically.
Transit hub
Central routing reduces attachments.
PrivateLink
Service interface via ENI and NLB.
Why it matters
Selecting the right connectivity pattern reduces routing complexity, improves security posture, and controls operational cost as your cloud estate grows.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of these lessons you will be able to evaluate connectivity options, configure and troubleshoot peering and Transit Gateway, design PrivateLink services, and reason about security and cost tradeoffs. The first objective is to evaluate and select between VPC Peering, Transit Gateway, and PrivateLink based on scale, required transitivity, and operational overhead. You’ll practice a second objective: configure and troubleshoot VPC Peering connections, remembering that peering is non‑transitive and both route tables must be updated. Third, you’ll implement and manage Transit Gateway attachments and route tables, including route propagation to simplify operations. Fourth, you’ll design and deploy PrivateLink endpoints and endpoint services so services can be consumed across accounts without the public internet. Each objective is paired with a small mnemonic or visual so you can remember when to use each technique. We’ll also present verification steps for each objective so you can confirm competency as you practice in the console. These skills directly affect how maintainable and secure large AWS networks become as you add accounts and services.

screens.title: VPC Peering: definition and behavior
screens.narratorSegment: VPC Peering connects two VPCs so instances can communicate as if on a single network. In plain terms, peering creates a direct private path between two VPCs, but it only links those two endpoints. A critical property to remember is non‑transitivity: if VPC A peers with VPC B, and VPC B peers with VPC C, traffic will not flow from A to C through B. This is not a bug; it’s a design constraint that prevents peering from forming an implicit mesh. A concrete example: if you peer a development VPC to a security VPC for logging, and also peer the security VPC to a production VPC, the development VPC cannot reach production through security VPC unless you create an explicit peering between development and production. A common misconception is thinking that peering automatically forwards traffic across multiple peer links — always confirm that both sides have explicit routes for the peer CIDR and that security groups allow the traffic. Key operational steps include creating the peering connection, accepting it in the other account or VPC, and then adding route table entries on both sides for the remote CIDR. Keep this mental model: peering is simple and low cost for a few VPCs, but its non‑transitive nature makes it fragile as the number of VPCs grows.

keyIdea.title: VPC Peering rule
keyIdea.text: Peering links only connect two VPCs and do not forward traffic beyond the peer — both route tables must include the peered CIDR.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › VPC Peering
Definition
Point‑to‑point VPC connectivity
Allows instances in two VPCs to communicate privately. Requires route table entries in both VPCs and does not forward traffic to other peers.
Explanation
  • Create peering, accept peer, update both VPC route tables with remote CIDR.
  • Security Groups and NACLs still govern allowed flows; routing alone is not enough.
  • Non‑transitive: peering does not act as a router between multiple peers.
Concrete example
VPC A (10.10.0.0/16) peers with VPC B (10.20.0.0/16). After acceptance, add a route in A to 10.20.0.0/16 via the peering connection, and add the reciprocal route in B. Confirm security groups allow the traffic, then test with an instance ping or application call.
Common mistake
Forgetting to add the remote CIDR to both route tables, or leaving Security Groups blocking the flow after peering is active.
Key Takeaway
Peering is simple and cost‑effective for a few VPCs but does not scale due to non‑transitivity.

screens.title: Peering at scale — mesh complexity and limits
screens.narratorSegment: When you have many VPCs, peering requires a direct connection between each pair you want to communicate. The formula for the number of peering links in a full mesh is N times N minus one, divided by two — that is, N*(N-1)/2 links for N VPCs. Practically, that means connections and route entries grow quadratically. For a handful of VPCs this is manageable; at tens of VPCs it becomes an operational burden. Consider 16 VPCs: a full mesh would need 120 peering connections and dozens of route table edits. A common misstep is assuming you can rely on a transit VPC to forward traffic between peers; peering does not provide transitive routing. Another operational pitfall is inconsistent route maintenance: one team may add a peering link but forget to update routes in all affected route tables. To make this concrete, imagine three teams each owning multiple VPCs. Each time a new VPC is created you must decide whether to peer it to many other VPCs or accept isolation. That operational choice drives the recommendation: use peering for a small number of straightforward connections, not for many VPCs. The takeaway: quantify the number of connections you’ll need before choosing peering, and prefer hub models when the number grows beyond a handful.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Peering at scale
Mesh math
N*(N-1)/2 connections
This formula gives the number of pairwise peering links needed for a full mesh. Each new VPC increases connections by N-1, where N is the resulting count of VPCs.
Operational implications
  • Route table updates across many VPCs create human error risks.
  • Security groups must be coordinated per connection, increasing policy sprawl.
  • Transitivity is not supported, so a mesh is the only way to allow arbitrary pairwise traffic.
Example
If you have 5 VPCs, full mesh peering requires 10 peering connections. Add VPC six and you jump to 15 connections. The management and troubleshooting effort increases sharply as you add VPCs.
Misconception
Assuming peering automatically forwards across peers leads to silent connectivity gaps. Always test pairwise reachability.
Key Takeaway
Peering is practical for a small set of VPCs; use hub approaches like Transit Gateway for many VPCs.

screens.title: AWS Transit Gateway (TGW)
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Transit Gateway provides a central hub that connects multiple VPCs and on‑premises networks so attachments can communicate transitively. Unlike peering, TGW supports transitive routing: attachments connected to the same TGW can reach one another subject to the TGW route tables. The architecture centers on three concepts: attachments, TGW route tables, and propagation. An attachment represents a VPC, VPN, Direct Connect gateway, or another transit gateway. Each attachment can be associated with a specific TGW route table, enabling segmentation. Route propagation allows the TGW to learn CIDRs from attachments automatically, which reduces manual route maintenance. A concrete example: attach AppVPC and DataVPC to a TGW, associate both with a default TGW route table, enable propagation so the TGW learns both VPC CIDRs, then update each VPC's route table to direct remote CIDRs to the TGW attachment. A common operational trap is misconfiguring associations versus propagations; associations control which attachments are visible to a route table and propagation controls which routes that table learns. The key operational benefit is reducing the number of connections from quadratic to linear with the number of VPCs, replacing a mesh with predictable attachments that are easier to manage and secure.

keyIdea.title: TGW architecture
keyIdea.text: TGW converts many-to-many connectivity into hub attachments, using route tables and propagation to control segmentation and reachability.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Transit Gateway
Architecture
Hub‑and‑spoke network transit
TGW attaches VPCs and other networks, then controls how traffic flows using TGW‑specific route tables and propagation.
Attachments
Connections from VPCs, VPNs, Direct Connect gateways, and other TGWs.
TGW Route Tables
Segment traffic by associating attachments with specific route tables.
Route Propagation
Automatically learn attachment CIDRs into a TGW route table to simplify management.
Concrete scenario
Attach AppVPC (10.10.0.0/16) and DataVPC (10.20.0.0/16) to a TGW. Associate both attachments with the default TGW route table and enable propagation so the TGW learns both CIDRs. Update each VPC route table to point 10.20.0.0/16 or 10.10.0.0/16 to the TGW attachment. Now instances can communicate transitively through the TGW, subject to TGW routing rules and security controls.
Misconception
Assuming VPC route tables alone determine cross‑VPC flow. Both VPC and TGW route tables must be correct for connectivity to work.
Key Takeaway
TGW simplifies many‑VPC topologies by centralizing routing and enabling segmentation via multiple TGW route tables.

screens.title: Transit Gateway route tables, associations, and propagation
screens.narratorSegment: Transit Gateway uses route tables that are distinct from VPC route tables to control how traffic flows between attachments. There are two separate controls you must understand: associations and propagations. Association ties an attachment to a specific TGW route table — this controls which route table the attachment consults when forwarding traffic. Propagation is how routes from attachments become known to a TGW route table; when you enable propagation from an attachment, the TGW learns the attachment’s CIDRs and can add them to the route table. A concrete example: create two TGW route tables named Production and Development. Associate production VPC attachments with the Production route table and development attachments with Development. Then configure propagation so that shared services attachments propagate routes into both route tables if desired. A frequent troubleshooting step is verifying that the correct attachment is both associated with the intended TGW route table and that propagation from peer attachments is enabled. If propagation is missing, the TGW will not have routes to the remote VPC CIDRs and traffic will be dropped even though attachments exist. Remember: associations select the view, propagation teaches the routes.

keyIdea.title: TGW routing concept
keyIdea.text: Associations select which route table an attachment uses; propagation teaches CIDRs into a TGW route table — both must be configured for intended reachability.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › TGW Routing
Concepts
Associations vs Propagation
Use associations to assign attachments to a TGW route table and propagation to allow a route table to learn attachment CIDRs automatically.
1. Create TGW route tables for segmentation e.g., Production and Development.
2. Associate attachments with the appropriate route table to control their view of other attachments.
3. Enable propagation from attachments you want the route table to learn automatically.
Troubleshooting prompts
If cross‑VPC traffic fails, check: VPC route tables point to the TGW attachment; the attachment is associated with the expected TGW route table; propagation is enabled for the remote attachment; and Security Groups permit traffic.
Example
Attach AppVPC to TGW and associate with Development route table. Ensure DataVPC propagates its CIDR into Development if you expect reachability.
Key Takeaway
Associations control which route table an attachment uses; propagation controls which routes that table learns — both are necessary for correct routing.

screens.title: Hands‑on: Create a Transit Gateway and attach two VPCs
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough follows the hands‑on activity in the chapter. The goal is to create a transit gateway, add attachments for two existing VPCs, configure the TGW route table with associations and propagation, and then update each VPC route table to point to the TGW. Start by creating the TGW resource in the VPC console and name it, for example, MyOrg‑TGW. Next create two Transit Gateway attachments: one for AppVPC and one for DataVPC. Select subnets in each Availability Zone for each attachment so the attachment has an ENI in each AZ. Wait until attachments reach the available state. Then open Transit Gateway route tables, select the default or create a named route table, and associate both attachments with it. Under propagations, add both attachments so the TGW learns each VPC CIDR. Finally, update the VPC route tables for AppVPC and DataVPC: add a route to the other VPC's CIDR with the TGW as the target. After these edits, verify connectivity by launching instances and testing ping or an application port, ensuring Security Groups allow the traffic. A common mistake is updating VPC routes but forgetting to create or accept the TGW attachments — both sides must be present and visible to the TGW route table.

keyIdea.title: Deployment checklist
keyIdea.text: Create TGW → attachments → TGW route table associations and propagations → update VPC route tables → validate security groups and test connectivity.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › TGW Hands‑on
Step sequence (console)
1. VPC Console → Transit Gateways → Create Transit Gateway (name: MyOrg-TGW) 2. Transit Gateway attachments → Create attachment → select MyOrg-TGW, choose AppVPC, select subnets in each AZ → Create 3. Repeat for DataVPC → wait until attachments show status 'available' 4. Transit Gateway route tables → select default or create new → Create association for both attachments 5. Under propagations → Create propagation for both attachments so TGW learns their CIDRs 6. VPC route tables → edit routes for AppVPC subnets → Add route: Destination 10.20.0.0/16 → Target: transit gateway ID 7. Repeat for DataVPC route tables → Destination 10.10.0.0/16 → Target: transit gateway ID 8. Launch instances and validate connectivity; check Security Groups and NACLs
Checks and example
After attachments are available and propagation is set, the TGW route table should list learned CIDRs for both attachments. The VPC route table entries should target the TGW ID. If ping fails, verify Security Groups allow ICMP or the relevant protocol. Also confirm that the TGW route table used by attachments contains the remote CIDR entries.
Pro tip
Use clear naming for attachments and route tables (e.g., AppVPC-Attachment) so associations and propagations are easy to audit.
Key Takeaway
A successful TGW deployment requires attachments, correct associations/propagations, VPC route updates, and security validation — all four are necessary.

screens.title: Troubleshooting common connectivity failures
screens.narratorSegment: When connectivity fails between VPCs, a disciplined checklist quickly finds the issue. Start by confirming routes exist: in peering, both VPC route tables must have routes for the remote CIDR via the peering connection. In TGW scenarios, both the VPC route tables and the TGW route table must include the intended routes, and the correct attachment must be associated with the TGW route table that contains the route. A concrete example: if AppVPC cannot reach DataVPC, check AppVPC route table for a route targeting the TGW, then open the TGW route table to confirm it has a route to DataVPC and that the AppVPC attachment is associated with that TGW route table. Next, examine Security Groups and NACLs; a common mistake is assuming routing alone opens access. Security Groups are stateful and must permit the required inbound traffic, while NACLs are stateless and must allow both directions. Another frequent error is missing TGW propagation — without propagation the TGW route table will not learn remote CIDRs and traffic is blackholed. Finally, confirm attachments are in the available state. By following this layered comparison and check sequence you reduce time to resolution and avoid chasing symptoms instead of root causes.

keyIdea.title: Troubleshoot flow
keyIdea.text: Check route tables (VPC and TGW), associations/propagations, attachment status, then Security Groups and NACLs in that order.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Troubleshooting
Stepwise checks
  1. Confirm VPC route tables point to the peer or TGW target.
  2. Confirm TGW route table has learned or contains the remote CIDR.
  3. Verify attachment is associated with the TGW route table that contains the route.
  4. Confirm attachment status is available.
  5. Check Security Groups and NACLs allow the expected traffic.
Example failure
An engineer updated the VPC route but forgot TGW propagation. The TGW route table lacked the remote CIDR, so traffic was dropped. Fixing propagation restored the learned route and connectivity returned. This illustrates why both VPC and TGW tables must be validated.
Common pitfall
Treating TGW like a single route table. Multiple TGW route tables may isolate attachments — confirm the correct table is referenced.
Key Takeaway
A structured checklist that validates routing, associations, propagation, and security shortens troubleshooting time.

screens.title: AWS PrivateLink: how it works
screens.narratorSegment: PrivateLink provides private connectivity for service consumption across VPCs and accounts without sending traffic over the public internet. The pattern relies on two principal components: the VPC Endpoint Service, created by the service provider, typically backed by a Network Load Balancer that fronts service instances; and the Interface VPC Endpoint, created by the consumer, which provisions ENIs with private IPs in the consumer subnets. When a consumer creates an interface endpoint for a provider’s service, traffic flows from the consumer's application to the endpoint ENI, then over the AWS private network to the provider's NLB and service instances. This isolates the service and avoids exposing any public IPs or requiring CIDR alignment. A concrete example: a SaaS provider exposes an A P I via an endpoint service in their account; your consumer VPC creates an interface endpoint and calls the service using private IPs. A common misconception is that PrivateLink replaces TGW or peering for general connectivity — PrivateLink is for service consumption, not arbitrary VPC routing. Endpoint policies, NACLs, and security groups on the interface ENI control access, so designing appropriate policies is essential to secure consumption.

keyIdea.text: PrivateLink exposes services via a provider NLB and consumer interface ENIs so traffic remains on the AWS private network without general VPC routing or CIDR coordination.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › PrivateLink
Definition
Private service connectivity
PrivateLink lets consumers call services privately using interface endpoints that appear as ENIs in the consumer VPC and route traffic to a provider’s NLB-backed service.
Components
  • VPC Endpoint Service — created by the service provider and backed by an NLB.
  • Interface VPC Endpoint — created by the consumer, appears as ENIs in subnets.
  • Endpoint policies and security groups control access.
Example
A provider publishes an API behind a Network Load Balancer and creates a VPC Endpoint Service. Your account creates an Interface Endpoint in your subnets. Your application sends requests to the interface ENI's private IP and traffic flows over the AWS private backbone to the provider's NLB and service instances, never touching the public internet.
Misconception
PrivateLink is not a general routing fabric; it exposes services, not arbitrary VPC subnets or internet egress.
Key Takeaway
Use PrivateLink for secure service consumption across accounts without public endpoints or CIDR coordination.

screens.title: PrivateLink traffic flow and security controls
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the flow of traffic through PrivateLink helps you design secure service integrations. Traffic originates in the consumer application, reaches the Interface Endpoint ENI inside the consumer VPC, and traverses the AWS private network to the provider’s Network Load Balancer. From the NLB the traffic reaches one of the provider’s service instances. Security controls exist at multiple points: the interface endpoint has security groups that can restrict inbound traffic to certain ports and IP ranges; endpoint policies can control which IAM principals are allowed to use the endpoint; and on the provider side, the NLB and service instances continue to enforce their own security groups. A concrete example is a central DNS resolver service exposed by a Security VPC: the provider publishes an endpoint service backed by an NLB; consuming VPCs create interface endpoints and attach security groups that allow DNS queries only from application subnets. A common misconception is assuming the endpoint alone enforces authorization — you must design endpoint policies and instance Security Groups together to achieve the intended access model. The practical benefit is that services are consumed without public IP exposure and without requiring peering or TGW attachments for each consumer.

keyIdea.title: PrivateLink security
keyIdea.text: Combine interface endpoint security groups and endpoint policies with provider NLB and instance controls to enforce least privilege for service consumers.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › PrivateLink Security
Traffic path
Application → Interface Endpoint ENI in consumer VPC → AWS private network → Provider NLB → Provider service instances. No public internet hop is required.
Interface Endpoint Security Groups: restrict which IPs and ports can use the endpoint.
Endpoint Policies: restrict which IAM principals or actions can call the service via the endpoint.
Provider side controls: NLB listeners and instance Security Groups enforce service access.
Example: Central DNS service
Security VPC exposes a resolver via a VPC Endpoint Service. Each consumer creates an interface endpoint and applies an SG allowing DNS from application subnets and an endpoint policy restricting which principals can use it. The resolver never needs a public IP and consumers don’t need peering or TGW attachments just to use the service.
Misconception
Assuming PrivateLink eliminates provider-side security responsibilities. Providers still need to secure their service instances and NLB listeners.
Key Takeaway
Use endpoint policies and SGs on the interface ENI plus provider controls to enforce least privilege for service consumption.

screens.title: Choosing between Peering, Transit Gateway, and PrivateLink
screens.narratorSegment: Selecting the right connectivity pattern depends on what you need: point‑to‑point connectivity, transitive hub networking, or private service exposure. Use VPC Peering for simple, low‑cost connections between two VPCs when you have a small number of links and no need for transitivity. Choose Transit Gateway when you need scalable many‑to‑many connectivity, central routing control, and the ability to attach on‑premises networks — it converts a mesh into a manageable hub but introduces TGW route tables and additional cost. Opt for PrivateLink when you want to publish a specific service to multiple consumers without exposing it on the public internet and without requiring full network connectivity; it’s ideal for SaaS or centrally provided services. A concrete scenario: a SharedServices VPC used by 15 Application VPCs is best connected via TGW because peering would require dozens of links and complex routing. If that SharedServices VPC instead provides only a specific A P I, PrivateLink could be used so each application consumes the A P I via interface endpoints without broad routing. Common errors in decision making include overusing peering where a hub would simplify operations, and treating PrivateLink as a replacement for general routing. The right choice reduces operational overhead and improves security posture.

keyIdea.title: Decision matrix
keyIdea.text: Peering for a few point‑to‑point links, TGW for scalable hub‑and‑spoke networks, PrivateLink for private service consumption.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Choosing connectivity
VPC Peering
Best for 1:1 or a very small set of connections. Low cost per link, non‑transitive, route tables must be updated on both sides.
Transit Gateway
Best for many VPCs and hybrid connectivity. Transitive hub, TGW route tables, attachments, propagation; easier to manage as scale grows.
PrivateLink
Best for exposing or consuming a specific service privately across accounts without general routing or CIDR coordination.
Scenario match
SharedServices VPC with many Application VPCs → Transit Gateway. Single API offered to many consumers without broad routing needs → PrivateLink. A few direct connections between known VPCs → VPC Peering.

screens.title: Scenario walk‑through: central Security VPC and egress inspection
screens.narratorSegment: Consider a Security VPC that hosts a centralized egress inspection appliance and multiple Application VPCs that must route internet‑bound traffic through it. If you used peering, each Application VPC would need a peering link to the Security VPC and specific route entries to forward traffic — this rapidly becomes unmanageable at scale. Transit Gateway is a better fit: attach all Application VPCs and the Security VPC to the TGW, configure a TGW route table so Application VPCs have a default route pointing to the TGW attachment, and then route via the TGW to the Security VPC. The Security VPC can then egress to the internet through its Internet Gateway. This centralizes inspection and routing, while simplifying additions of new Application VPCs. PrivateLink is an alternative only when the Security VPC offers a discrete service, such as a threat intelligence feed or DNS resolver. In that case, you can publish an endpoint service and have Application VPCs create interface endpoints, using security groups and endpoint policies to restrict access. The takeaway is to match the pattern to whether you need full egress routing (use TGW) or only service consumption (use PrivateLink).

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Security VPC scenario
Problem
Multiple Application VPCs must send internet‑bound traffic to a central Security VPC for inspection before egress.
With peering you would need one peering link per Application VPC and manual routing to the Security VPC. With a Transit Gateway you attach each VPC once and configure TGW routing so traffic from all application spokes is forwarded to the security spoke, which then egresses to the internet gateway.
Alternatives
If the Security VPC only exposes a specific service such as a DNS resolver, PrivateLink lets customers consume that service via interface endpoints. For full egress routing and inspection, Transit Gateway is the practical choice.
Key Takeaway
Match the pattern: TGW for centralized routing and inspection, PrivateLink for discrete service consumption without broad routing.

screens.title: Key Concepts

VPC Peering creates a private, direct link between two VPCs and is non‑transitive, which makes it suitable for a small number of point‑to‑point connections. AWS Transit Gateway is a transitive hub that connects multiple VPCs and on‑premises networks using attachments and TGW route tables; use it for scalable hub‑and‑spoke architectures. PrivateLink exposes specific services across VPCs using a provider VPC Endpoint Service backed by an NLB and a consumer Interface VPC Endpoint that appears as ENIs; it keeps service traffic on the AWS private network without requiring broad routing or CIDR coordination. Keep these three cards in mind as decision points: peering for simplicity, TGW for scale, PrivateLink for private service exposure. When designing, always validate both routing and security controls and choose the pattern that minimizes operational complexity while meeting security and compliance needs.

Transit Gateway Attachments

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we’re going to build a mental model for three ways AWS lets VPCs talk to each other: VPC Peering, Transit Gateway, and PrivateLink. I’ll help you see where each service fits, what operational work they demand, and where people commonly make mistakes. You’ll learn a concrete example that shows why a small mesh of peering connections becomes painful at scale, how Transit Gateway centralizes routing for hub‑and‑spoke architectures, and when PrivateLink is the right way to expose a service securely across accounts without opening public endpoints. This matters because the connectivity method you choose affects cost, manageability, and security controls. For instance, a simple peering link is cheap and direct for two VPCs but quickly multiplies routing work as the environment grows. Transit Gateway reduces that operational cost at the price of centralized configuration and higher service cost. PrivateLink moves traffic over AWS private networks to present a service via an interface endpoint, avoiding CIDR coordination and public exposure. As you move through the screens you’ll see the essential configuration steps, common troubleshooting checks, and a hands‑on scenario that ties these ideas together. By the end you should be able to pick the right connectivity option for a real multi‑account architecture and explain why.

By the end of these lessons you will be able to evaluate connectivity options, configure and troubleshoot peering and Transit Gateway, design PrivateLink services, and reason about security and cost tradeoffs. The first objective is to evaluate and select between VPC Peering, Transit Gateway, and PrivateLink based on scale, required transitivity, and operational overhead. You’ll practice a second objective: configure and troubleshoot VPC Peering connections, remembering that peering is non‑transitive and both route tables must be updated. Third, you’ll implement and manage Transit Gateway attachments and route tables, including route propagation to simplify operations. Fourth, you’ll design and deploy PrivateLink endpoints and endpoint services so services can be consumed across accounts without the public internet. Each objective is paired with a small mnemonic or visual so you can remember when to use each technique. We’ll also present verification steps for each objective so you can confirm competency as you practice in the console. These skills directly affect how maintainable and secure large AWS networks become as you add accounts and services.

This second objectives slide emphasizes verification and analysis skills. You will learn to analyze security and cost implications of each connectivity method. For example, you will compare the management overhead of maintaining dozens of peering connections to the centralized control offered by a Transit Gateway and weigh that against TGW service costs. You will also gain skills in endpoint policy design and security group configuration for PrivateLink so you can restrict which principals and resources may connect to a provided service. The learning activities ask you to create TGW attachments and to add routes in both the VPC route tables and TGW route table, then validate connectivity with simple instance tests. Finally, we emphasize troubleshooting: always check both sides of a peering route, check TGW associations and propagations, and confirm Security Groups and NACLs permit the expected traffic. These verification steps are what turns configuration into proven competency in a real account.

VPC Peering connects two VPCs so instances can communicate as if on a single network. In plain terms, peering creates a direct private path between two VPCs, but it only links those two endpoints. A critical property to remember is non‑transitivity: if VPC A peers with VPC B, and VPC B peers with VPC C, traffic will not flow from A to C through B. This is not a bug; it’s a design constraint that prevents peering from forming an implicit mesh. A concrete example: if you peer a development VPC to a security VPC for logging, and also peer the security VPC to a production VPC, the development VPC cannot reach production through security VPC unless you create an explicit peering between development and production. A common misconception is thinking that peering automatically forwards traffic across multiple peer links — always confirm that both sides have explicit routes for the peer CIDR and that security groups allow the traffic. Key operational steps include creating the peering connection, accepting it in the other account or VPC, and then adding route table entries on both sides for the remote CIDR. Keep this mental model: peering is simple and low cost for a few VPCs, but its non‑transitive nature makes it fragile as the number of VPCs grows.

When you have many VPCs, peering requires a direct connection between each pair you want to communicate. The formula for the number of peering links in a full mesh is N times N minus one, divided by two — that is, N*(N-1)/2 links for N VPCs. Practically, that means connections and route entries grow quadratically. For a handful of VPCs this is manageable; at tens of VPCs it becomes an operational burden. Consider 16 VPCs: a full mesh would need 120 peering connections and dozens of route table edits. A common misstep is assuming you can rely on a transit VPC to forward traffic between peers; peering does not provide transitive routing. Another operational pitfall is inconsistent route maintenance: one team may add a peering link but forget to update routes in all affected route tables. To make this concrete, imagine three teams each owning multiple VPCs. Each time a new VPC is created you must decide whether to peer it to many other VPCs or accept isolation. That operational choice drives the recommendation: use peering for a small number of straightforward connections, not for many VPCs. The takeaway: quantify the number of connections you’ll need before choosing peering, and prefer hub models when the number grows beyond a handful.

AWS Transit Gateway provides a central hub that connects multiple VPCs and on‑premises networks so attachments can communicate transitively. Unlike peering, TGW supports transitive routing: attachments connected to the same TGW can reach one another subject to the TGW route tables. The architecture centers on three concepts: attachments, TGW route tables, and propagation. An attachment represents a VPC, VPN, Direct Connect gateway, or another transit gateway. Each attachment can be associated with a specific TGW route table, enabling segmentation. Route propagation allows the TGW to learn CIDRs from attachments automatically, which reduces manual route maintenance. A concrete example: attach AppVPC and DataVPC to a TGW, associate both with a default TGW route table, enable propagation so the TGW learns both VPC CIDRs, then update each VPC's route table to direct remote CIDRs to the TGW attachment. A common operational trap is misconfiguring associations versus propagations; associations control which attachments are visible to a route table and propagation controls which routes that table learns. The key operational benefit is reducing the number of connections from quadratic to linear with the number of VPCs, replacing a mesh with predictable attachments that are easier to manage and secure.

Transit Gateway uses route tables that are distinct from VPC route tables to control how traffic flows between attachments. There are two separate controls you must understand: associations and propagations. Association ties an attachment to a specific TGW route table — this controls which route table the attachment consults when forwarding traffic. Propagation is how routes from attachments become known to a TGW route table; when you enable propagation from an attachment, the TGW learns the attachment’s CIDRs and can add them to the route table. A concrete example: create two TGW route tables named Production and Development. Associate production VPC attachments with the Production route table and development attachments with Development. Then configure propagation so that shared services attachments propagate routes into both route tables if desired. A frequent troubleshooting step is verifying that the correct attachment is both associated with the intended TGW route table and that propagation from peer attachments is enabled. If propagation is missing, the TGW will not have routes to the remote VPC CIDRs and traffic will be dropped even though attachments exist. Remember: associations select the view, propagation teaches the routes.

This walkthrough follows the hands‑on activity in the chapter. The goal is to create a transit gateway, add attachments for two existing VPCs, configure the TGW route table with associations and propagation, and then update each VPC route table to point to the TGW. Start by creating the TGW resource in the VPC console and name it, for example, MyOrg‑TGW. Next create two Transit Gateway attachments: one for AppVPC and one for DataVPC. Select subnets in each Availability Zone for each attachment so the attachment has an ENI in each AZ. Wait until attachments reach the available state. Then open Transit Gateway route tables, select the default or create a named route table, and associate both attachments with it. Under propagations, add both attachments so the TGW learns each VPC CIDR. Finally, update the VPC route tables for AppVPC and DataVPC: add a route to the other VPC's CIDR with the TGW as the target. After these edits, verify connectivity by launching instances and testing ping or an application port, ensuring Security Groups allow the traffic. A common mistake is updating VPC routes but forgetting to create or accept the TGW attachments — both sides must be present and visible to the TGW route table.

When connectivity fails between VPCs, a disciplined checklist quickly finds the issue. Start by confirming routes exist: in peering, both VPC route tables must have routes for the remote CIDR via the peering connection. In TGW scenarios, both the VPC route tables and the TGW route table must include the intended routes, and the correct attachment must be associated with the TGW route table that contains the route. A concrete example: if AppVPC cannot reach DataVPC, check AppVPC route table for a route targeting the TGW, then open the TGW route table to confirm it has a route to DataVPC and that the AppVPC attachment is associated with that TGW route table. Next, examine Security Groups and NACLs; a common mistake is assuming routing alone opens access. Security Groups are stateful and must permit the required inbound traffic, while NACLs are stateless and must allow both directions. Another frequent error is missing TGW propagation — without propagation the TGW route table will not learn remote CIDRs and traffic is blackholed. Finally, confirm attachments are in the available state. By following this layered comparison and check sequence you reduce time to resolution and avoid chasing symptoms instead of root causes.

PrivateLink exposes specific services across VPCs using a provider VPC Endpoint Service backed by an NLB and a consumer Interface VPC Endpoint that appears as ENIs; it keeps service traffic on the AWS private network without requiring broad routing or CIDR coordination. Keep these three cards in mind as decision points: peering for simplicity, TGW for scale, PrivateLink for private service exposure. When designing, always validate both routing and security controls and choose the pattern that minimizes operational complexity while meeting security and compliance needs.

These compact concept cards list the technical terms you’ve seen. Transit Gateway attachments are the entities that connect VPCs, VPNs, and Direct Connect to the TGW. Transit Gateway route tables are distinct, TGW‑level routing domains used to segment traffic and control which attachments can reach others. Finally, the PrivateLink pair: VPC Endpoint Service (provider) backed by a Network Load Balancer, and Interface VPC Endpoints (consumer) that appear as ENIs in the consumer VPC.
